100	Four findings emerge. First, intra-batch substitution scales monotonically with BCS in both tasks: NER IntraSub rises from 0\% (solo) to 49.4\% (high BCS) with $\rho = 1.0$ ($p < 0.001$), and RE IntraSub rises from 0\% through 20.3\% (high) to 32.3\% (very high) with $\rho = 0.954$ ($p < 10^{-6}$). Second, 100\% of type confusion errors in RE are intra-batch---the model exclusively confuses types present in the current prompt, never hallucinating types outside the schema. Third, RE missed-entity rates remain relatively flat across BCS bins (10.4--15.7\%), confirming that for relation extraction, confusability drives type confusion independently of detection failure. Fourth, NER exhibits a strikingly different pattern: missed rates are substantially higher (42.8--64.8\%) and non-monotonic across BCS bins. This divergence suggests that in span-level extraction, confusable type sets impair not only type discrimination but also entity detection itself---possibly because semantically similar types share ambiguous entity boundaries, causing the model to abstain rather than commit to a confusable label.

tool_args.new_string:
\section*{Limitations}
All experiments use a single primary model (Qwen3-32B); cross-model validation is ongoing. The pairwise confusability signal explains roughly 1.3--1.7\% of the variance in type confusion---entity frequency, prompt position effects, and type definition quality account for the remainder. Our decomposition experiments test only union-based merge strategies; calibration-aware or joint-decoding alternatives remain unexplored. We conducted a within-dataset $2\!\times\!2$ factorial analysis (count $\times$ BCS) on Few-NERD; the interaction term was directionally consistent but not statistically significant ($z = -0.67$, $p = 0.50$), possibly due to BCS range compression in high-count schemas. The primary evidence for count--confusability interaction remains the $3.4\times$ amplification observed across FewRel schema scales (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).

tool_args.old_string:
We presented a controlled empirical study isolating schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM IE into two channels: a count channel suppressing recall as candidate types increase, and a confusability channel triggering intra-batch substitution errors between semantically similar types. These channels are cleanly separable in RE but interact in NER, where confusable type sets additionally impair entity detection. Pairwise SCS is a partial but robust predictor ($r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$), replicating across three tasks and two embedding spaces---the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE experiments. We further identify a centrality confound that reverses per-type aggregation on same-domain schemas, relevant to any embedding-based schema analysis.

Our SDGD experiments yield an informative negative result: merge amplification destroys precision across all decomposition strategies, a structural bottleneck for decompose-then-merge pipelines. Addressing this via cross-batch calibration or joint decoding is the key next step.
tool_args.new_string:
We presented a controlled empirical study isolating schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM IE into two channels: a count channel suppressing recall as candidate types increase, and a confusability channel triggering intra-batch substitution errors between semantically similar types. These channels are cleanly separable in RE but interact in NER, where confusable type sets additionally impair entity detection. The confusability effect amplifies with schema complexity ($3.4\times$ between 16-type and 80-type schemas). Pairwise SCS is a partial but robust predictor ($r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$ over $n{=}1{,}953$ type pairs; at the batch level, BCS-controlled accuracy gaps reach 31.2 percentage points), replicating across three tasks and two embedding spaces---the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE experiments. Entity frequency, prompt position effects, and type definition quality likely contribute to the remaining variance but have not been individually quantified. We further identify a centrality confound that reverses per-type aggregation on same-domain schemas, relevant to any embedding-based schema analysis.

Our SDGD experiments yield an informative negative result: merge amplification destroys precision across all decomposition strategies, suggesting a structural bottleneck that may generalize to decompose-then-merge pipelines beyond the single task and model tested here. Addressing this via cross-batch calibration or joint decoding is the key next step.

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{Limitations and open questions.}
Several limitations bound the scope of our findings. All primary experiments use Qwen3-32B; preliminary LLaMA-3.1-8B results replicate the count-degradation pattern (recall: $0.70 \to 0.27$, per-batch correlation with Qwen3: $r = 0.72$), but full cross-model BCS-controlled validation is ongoing. Our within-dataset $2\!\times\!2$ factorial analysis on Few-NERD did not reach statistical significance ($z = -0.67$, $p = 0.50$), possibly due to BCS range compression at high type counts; the cross-scale $3.4\times$ amplification on FewRel remains the primary interaction evidence. We did not test intermediate schema sizes (e.g., 40 relations) between the 16- and 80-relation FewRel experiments, leaving the shape of the scaling curve underspecified. Finally, SCS/BCS relies on embedding cosine similarity; alternative confusability metrics---such as label entropy, ontological depth, or empirical confusion priors---may capture complementary dimensions of schema difficulty.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
Preliminary LLaMA-3.1-8B results replicate Channel~1: recall drops from $0.70$ to $0.27$ with increasing count, with per-batch correlation $r = 0.72$ against Qwen3 rankings. Full BCS-controlled cross-model validation is ongoing; we report additional limitations in the Limitations section.

tool_args.old_string:
We presented a controlled empirical study isolating schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM IE into two channels: a count channel suppressing recall as candidate types increase, and a confusability channel triggering intra-batch substitution errors between semantically similar types. These channels are cleanly separable in RE but interact in NER, where confusable type sets additionally impair entity detection. The confusability effect amplifies with schema complexity ($3.4\times$ between 16-type and 80-type schemas). Pairwise SCS is a partial but robust predictor ($r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$ over $n{=}1{,}953$ type pairs; at the batch level, BCS-controlled accuracy gaps reach 31.2 percentage points), replicating across three tasks and two embedding spaces---the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE experiments. Entity frequency, prompt position effects, and type definition quality likely contribute to the remaining variance but have not been individually quantified. We further identify a centrality confound that reverses per-type aggregation on same-domain schemas, relevant to any embedding-based schema analysis.

Our SDGD experiments yield an informative negative result: merge amplification destroys precision across all decomposition strategies, suggesting a structural bottleneck that may generalize to decompose-then-merge pipelines beyond the single task and model tested here. Addressing this via cross-batch calibration or joint decoding is the key next step.
tool_args.new_string: We presented a controlled empirical study isolating schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM IE into two channels: a count channel suppressing recall, and a confusability channel triggering intra-batch substitution errors. These channels are cleanly separable in RE but interact in NER (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Pairwise SCS is a partial but robust predictor ($r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$), replicating across three tasks and two embedding spaces---the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE experiments. We further identify a centrality confound that reverses per-type aggregation on same-domain schemas. Our SDGD experiments yield an informative negative result: merge amplification destroys precision, suggesting a structural bottleneck for decompose-then-merge pipelines. Addressing this via cross-batch calibration or joint decoding is the key next step.

41	\citet{llm-pee-2025} independently proposed similarity-based partitioning for event extraction.
